# Messaging and event streams {#sec-messaging-and-event-streams}

A message lets one part of a system hand work or news to another without waiting for it. The photo service of the earlier chapters already needs
this: an upload must return quickly, but thumbnails, feed entries and search entries must still be made. Xu introduces the message queue as the tool
for exactly this, "a durable component ... that supports asynchronous communication. It serves as a buffer and distributes asynchronous requests"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Message queue"]. This chapter defines queues, topics and logs, what they promise about delivery and order,
how they fail, and how a log of events can itself be the record of a system's state.

The claims are of two kinds. Queues, topics, delivery semantics, the partitioned log, failure handling and event sourcing are definitions. Five
propositions with complete proofs make them quantitative: how a backlog grows and drains, when duplicate deliveries do no harm, how a consumer
group shares partitions and what order and duplicates it gives, what retries and a dead-letter queue cost, and how a state is rebuilt from a log.
The queueing results of chapter 3 are used by link.

The sources are the benchmark books, @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 1], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024
[Ch. 7], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 3.3, 4.6 and 5.1-5.4], @gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024 [Ch. 3],
@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Chs. 4-5], @pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024 [Chs. 2, 3 and 8] and
@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Chs. 5 and 7], with two papers: @kreps2011kafka on the Kafka log and @saltzer1984end on the end-to-end
argument.

The chapter has six sections. @sec-async defines queues and workers and proves how a backlog grows and drains. @sec-pubsub defines topics and
publish-subscribe. @sec-delivery defines delivery semantics and idempotence and proves when duplicates do no harm. @sec-partitioned-log defines
the partitioned log and proves what a consumer group guarantees. @sec-failure-handling defines retries, dead-letter queues and backpressure and
proves what retries cost. @sec-event-sourcing defines event sourcing, CQRS and change data capture and proves how state is rebuilt from a log.

The running example is the photo service's uploads: $2 \times 10^7$ a day, $231$ per second on average and $694$ per second in the busiest hour,
three times the mean (@exm-req-workload-assumptions). Each upload makes a thumbnail, assumed to take $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ of a worker's time, and its
event is read by the feed, search and notification services.

Every definition and proposition is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise with a hidden solution in two tabs: the argument,
then a computation with its recorded output. The computations run in plain Python 3.12 with NumPy, SimPy and the standard library's `sqlite3`;
queues, logs and consumers are simulated with seeded random numbers. Diagrams are written in the D2 language. Client code for particular brokers
is shown as illustrative code and is not run.

## Asynchronous work and queues {#sec-async}

A request that starts a long task need not wait for the task to finish. Liu draws the line by what the caller waits for: "in a synchronous call, the
user waits for the task result, whereas in an asynchronous call, the user does not wait for the task result" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Synchronous and Asynchronous"]. This section defines messages, queues, workers and backlog, and proves how a backlog grows when work arrives
faster than the workers can do it, and how fast it drains afterwards.

For more on this topic, see @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 1, "Message queue"], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Asynchronous Processing"
and "Custom Queue"], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 7, "Designing a distributed queue"] and @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Ch. 5,
pp. 178-179].

### Calls, messages and queues

Asynchronous work needs a place to wait. A queue holds it until a worker takes it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-message-queue}
#### Messages, queues and workers

1. A call is **synchronous** if the caller waits for the result of the task it starts, and **asynchronous** if it continues once the task has been
   handed over, learning the result later or not at all.
2. A **message** is a unit of data that one component sends for another to process. A **producer** creates messages, a **consumer** processes
   them, and a **broker** stores them between the two. A **message queue** is a broker that keeps each message until a consumer has processed it.
3. Consumers that take messages from one queue are **workers**, and together they form a **worker pool**: each message is given to one worker.
4. A consumer **acknowledges** a message to tell the broker that it has processed it. The broker then removes the message; a message that is not
   acknowledged may be given out again.
5. The **backlog** $B(t)$ of a queue at time $t$ is the number of messages that have arrived and not yet been processed, whether waiting or in
   processing.
:::

::::

Items 2 and 3 follow the benchmark books. Xu describes the parts: "Input services, called producers/publishers, create messages, and publish them
to a message queue. Other services or servers, called consumers/subscribers, connect to the queue, and perform actions defined by the messages"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Message queue"]. Tan gives the one-worker rule: "Each message is processed only once by a single consumer"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 4.6.2, p. 95]. Item 4 is Reis's: "The subscriber acknowledges receipt of the message, removing it from the
queue" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 5, p. 178].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Xu's own example is a photo service. It is the running example's thumbnail step.

::: {#exm-wq-xu-photo}
#### Photo processing workers

Web servers "publish photo processing jobs to the message queue. Photo processing workers pick up jobs from the message queue and
asynchronously perform photo customization tasks. The producer and the consumer can be scaled independently. When the size of the queue
becomes large, more workers are added" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Message queue"]. In the photo service the upload handler is the
producer, the message is "make the thumbnail of photo $x$", and the thumbnail service is the worker pool.
:::

Whether a call is synchronous depends on where its task is taken to end. Liu's checkout shows two choices.

::: {#exm-wq-liu-checkout}
#### Where the synchronous part ends

Checkout has three steps: click, charge, ship. If the call ends at the click, "the user and the browser client will not wait for steps 2
to 3", which gives "a better perceived latency" but "a poorer user experience if the payment processor fails"; if it ends at the charge, a
declined card is reported at once [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Synchronous and Asynchronous"]. In item 1's terms the same
request is asynchronous with respect to shipping in both designs, and synchronous with respect to payment only in the second.
:::

A common split makes only the enqueue synchronous. The caller then learns whether the work was accepted.

::: {#exm-wq-liu-tweet}
#### Synchronous up to the queue

For a trending-topics design, "the request to insert into the queue is synchronous, and everything post queue insertion is asynchronous.
This architecture means that if the request fails to insert into the queue, the user will get a message saying, 'Sorry you're unable to tweet
now, please try again'" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Reasons for Asynchronous Processing"]. The photo service does the same: an
upload returns once the photo is stored and the thumbnail message is in the queue.
:::

A queue lets producer and consumer run at different times. Neither needs the other to be up.

::: {#exm-wq-xu-decoupling}
#### Decoupling in time

"With the message queue, the producer can post a message to the queue when the consumer is unavailable to process it. The consumer can
read messages from the queue even when the producer is unavailable" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Message queue"]. A synchronous
call needs both ends up at once; with a queue each end needs only itself and the broker.
:::

A pool can be simulated without threads. Two workers take turns at the head of one queue.

::: {#exm-wq-pool-code}
#### A worker pool in code

The run gives six messages to two workers. Each message goes to exactly one of them (item 3).

```{.python .run}
from collections import deque
queue = deque(f"thumb:{i}" for i in range(6))
done = {"w0": [], "w1": []}
turn = 0
while queue:
    worker = f"w{turn % 2}"
    done[worker].append(queue.popleft())   # taking a message removes it for everyone
    turn += 1
for w, msgs in done.items():
    print(w, msgs)
```

```{.text .run-output}
w0 ['thumb:0', 'thumb:2', 'thumb:4']
w1 ['thumb:1', 'thumb:3', 'thumb:5']
```
:::

Liu lists when to make work asynchronous. Each reason is about what the user should not wait for.

::: {#exm-wq-liu-reasons}
#### Reasons for asynchronous work

The nature of the job is asynchronous (a crawler with no waiting user), the processing time is "indeterministic" (matching a rider with a
driver), the processing is "long-running" (an order that takes two days, a movie that takes an hour to transcode), or asynchrony improves
"perceived latency" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Reasons for Asynchronous Processing"]. Thumbnails are long-running relative to
an upload request, and no user waits for them.
:::

Sinha lists three advantages of queues. They are buffering, decoupling and redelivery.

::: {#exm-wq-sinha-advantages}
#### What a queue gives

Queues help with "load management ... This buffering allows for handling bursts of messages without overwhelming the system", with
"decoupling system components", and with reliability: "If a consumer fails to process a message, the queue can redeliver it, ensuring data
consistency" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 7, "The advantages of using queues"]. Redelivery is item 4: an unacknowledged message is
given out again.
:::

A queue that keeps messages in one machine's memory loses them when it crashes. Reis puts the durability in replication.

::: {#exm-wq-reis-durable}
#### Durable by replication

"The message queue buffers messages to handle transient load spikes and makes messages durable through a distributed architecture with
replication" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 5, p. 178]. Xu's phrase "durable component, stored in memory" needs the same
reading: memory on several machines, as in the replication of @def-leader-follower.
:::

A queue need not be a separate product. Liu describes one made of a table with a status column.

::: {#exm-wq-sqlite-queue}
#### A queue in a table

One may "have a table of event_id and status, and you grab all the events in the pending stage" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Custom Queue"]. The run claims the oldest pending row and marks it done.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE jobs (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, photo TEXT, status TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO jobs (photo, status) VALUES (?, 'pending')", [("p1",), ("p2",), ("p3",)])
def claim():
    row = db.execute("SELECT id, photo FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1").fetchone()
    db.execute("UPDATE jobs SET status = 'done' WHERE id = ?", (row[0],))
    return row[1]
print(claim(), claim())
print(db.execute("SELECT photo, status FROM jobs ORDER BY id").fetchall())
```

```{.text .run-output}
p1 p2
[('p1', 'done'), ('p2', 'done'), ('p3', 'pending')]
```
:::

The running example's rates set the size of the pool. A thumbnail takes a fifth of a second.

::: {#exm-wq-photo-rates}
#### The photo service's thumbnail queue

Uploads arrive at $2 \times 10^7/86400 = 231$ per second on average and $694$ in the busiest hour. A worker making one thumbnail in
$0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ completes $\mu = 5$ per second, so the pool needs at least $139$ workers at the peak and $47$ on average; the user's upload
waits only for the enqueue.

```{.python .run}
mean = 2e7 / 86400
peak = 3 * mean
mu = 1 / 0.2
print(f"mean {mean:.0f}/s, peak {peak:.0f}/s, workers needed: mean {mean / mu:.1f}, peak {peak / mu:.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean 231/s, peak 694/s, workers needed: mean 46.3, peak 138.9
```
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise follows a declined card through Liu's two designs. The scope decides who learns of the failure, and when.

::: {#exr-wq-scope}
#### Two checkout scopes

In Liu's checkout (@exm-wq-liu-checkout), the card is declined. Describe what the user sees in each design, and how many requests the user
makes in all to complete the order with a second card.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

If the call ends at the click, the user is told the order is being processed; later a notification reports the failure, and the user returns
and places the order again: two checkout requests and a delay. If the call ends at the charge, the response itself says the card was declined and
the user retries at once: also two requests, but no delay and no notification. Both designs leave shipping asynchronous.

## Python

Both flows, step by step.

```{.python .run}
def checkout(scope, card_ok):
    msgs = []
    if scope == "click":
        msgs.append("response: processing your order")
        if not card_ok: msgs.append("later notification: payment failed, please order again")
    else:
        msgs.append("response: charged" if card_ok else "response: card declined, try another")
    return msgs
for scope in ("click", "charge"):
    print(scope, checkout(scope, False) + checkout(scope, True))
```

```{.text .run-output}
click ['response: processing your order', 'later notification: payment failed, please order again', 'response: processing your order']
charge ['response: card declined, try another', 'response: charged']
```
::::
:::

The second exercise prices the synchronous design. The user waits for every step it includes.

::: {#exr-wq-latency}
#### Upload latency

An upload stores the photo in $300\,\mathrm{ms}$. Making the thumbnails in three sizes takes $200\,\mathrm{ms}$ each, and an enqueue takes
$5\,\mathrm{ms}$. Find the upload's latency when the thumbnails are made inside the request and when only their message is enqueued.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Synchronously the user waits $300 + 3 \cdot 200 = 900\,\mathrm{ms}$; asynchronously $300 + 5 = 305\,\mathrm{ms}$. The thumbnail work is the
same in both; it moves out of the request.

## Python

The two sums.

```{.python .run}
store, thumb, enqueue = 300, 200, 5
print("synchronous", store + 3 * thumb, "ms; asynchronous", store + enqueue, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
synchronous 900 ms; asynchronous 305 ms
```
::::
:::

The third exercise puts decoupling in numbers. A synchronous chain fails when any link fails.

::: {#exr-wq-availability}
#### Availability with and without a queue

A producer, a broker and a consumer each have availability $0.999$, failing independently. Using @prp-series-parallel-availability,
compare the availability of a request that calls the consumer synchronously with one that only enqueues.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The synchronous request needs producer and consumer, $0.999^2 = 0.998$; the asynchronous one needs producer and broker, also $0.998$. The gain
is not in this number but in what fails: with the queue, a consumer outage delays work instead of failing requests, and the consumer's
availability drops out of the request path entirely.

## Python

The products, and the requests that fail during a consumer outage.

```{.python .run}
a = 0.999
print(f"sync {a * a:.6f}, async {a * a:.6f}")
print("requests failed during a 10-minute consumer outage at 694/s: sync", 694 * 600, ", async 0 (delayed)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
sync 0.998001, async 0.998001
requests failed during a 10-minute consumer outage at 694/s: sync 416400 , async 0 (delayed)
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise breaks item 3. Two workers that read before they remove can both take one message.

::: {#exr-wq-one-worker}
#### Taking a message atomically

Two workers take messages in two steps, "read the head" and "remove the head". Give an interleaving in which one message is processed twice and
another skipped, and say what makes item 3 hold.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Both read the head $m_1$, then both remove the head: $m_1$ is processed twice and $m_2$ is removed unprocessed. Item 3 holds when reading and
removing are one atomic step of the broker, as `popleft` is in @exm-wq-pool-code, or as a conditional update is in a table.

## Python

The bad interleaving.

```{.python .run}
queue = ["m1", "m2", "m3"]
w0 = queue[0]; w1 = queue[0]        # both read the head
queue.pop(0); queue.pop(0)          # both remove the head
print("processed:", w0, w1, "| left:", queue)
```

```{.text .run-output}
processed: m1 m1 | left: ['m3']
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise makes the table queue safe for two workers. A conditional update succeeds for only one of them.

::: {#exr-wq-sqlite-claim}
#### Claiming a row once

In @exm-wq-sqlite-queue, two workers may select the same pending row. Change the claim so that it succeeds for only one, and show it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Claim with `UPDATE jobs SET status = 'taken' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'pending'` and check the number of changed rows: the first worker
changes one row, the second changes none and selects again. The check and the change are one statement, so they are atomic.

## Python

Two workers race for row 1.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE jobs (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO jobs (status) VALUES (?)", [("pending",)] * 2)
def try_claim(row_id):
    return db.execute("UPDATE jobs SET status = 'taken' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'pending'", (row_id,)).rowcount
print("worker A:", try_claim(1), "row; worker B:", try_claim(1), "rows")
```

```{.text .run-output}
worker A: 1 row; worker B: 0 rows
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise sizes the thumbnail pool. Utilisation below one is not enough for short waits.

::: {#exr-wq-workers-80}
#### Workers for a target utilisation

Find the number of workers that keeps the thumbnail pool of @exm-wq-photo-rates at a utilisation of at most $0.8$ in the busiest hour.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $c$ workers the utilisation is $\rho = \lambda/(c\mu)$ (@thm-erlang-c), so $c \geq 694/(0.8 \cdot 5) = 173.6$: $174$ workers.

## Python

The bound.

```{.python .run}
import math
lam, mu = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 5
c = math.ceil(lam / (0.8 * mu))
print(c, "workers, utilisation", round(lam / (c * mu), 3))
```

```{.text .run-output}
174 workers, utilisation 0.798
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise compares two signals for adding workers. The same length means different waits for different pools.

::: {#exr-wq-age}
#### Length or age

Xu adds workers "when the size of the queue becomes large". A queue holds $1000$ messages. Find the wait of a newly arrived message, in a
first-in first-out queue, for a pool of $10$ workers and of $200$ workers at $5$ messages per second each. What signal measures the wait
directly?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The messages ahead are done at the pool's rate $c\mu$, so the new message waits $1000/50 = 20\,\mathrm{s}$ with ten workers and
$1000/1000 = 1\,\mathrm{s}$ with two hundred. The age of the oldest message measures the wait directly, whatever the pool's size.

## Python

Both pools.

```{.python .run}
for c in (10, 200):
    print(c, "workers: wait", 1000 / (5 * c), "s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
10 workers: wait 20.0 s
200 workers: wait 1.0 s
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise counts what a crash destroys. Little's law gives the number in the queue.

::: {#exr-wq-memory-loss}
#### What a memory-only queue loses

A broker keeps the thumbnail messages only in one machine's memory. In the busiest hour messages spend $2\,\mathrm{s}$ on average in it. How
many messages does a crash lose on average?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By Little's law (@thm-littles-law) the mean number present is $L = \lambda W = 694 \times 2 \approx 1389$; a crash at a random time loses
that many on average. Replication (@exm-wq-reis-durable) is what makes the queue durable.

## Python

The product.

```{.python .run}
lam, W = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 2.0
print(f"lost on average: {lam * W:.0f} messages")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lost on average: 1389 messages
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise follows item 4 through a crash. The broker cannot tell a slow worker from a dead one.

::: {#exr-wq-crash-before-ack}
#### A crash before the acknowledgement

A worker makes a thumbnail, writes it, and crashes before acknowledging the message. What happens to the message, and how many thumbnails are
written?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The message is not acknowledged, so the broker gives it out again; a second worker makes and writes the thumbnail again. Two writes of the same
thumbnail: harmless here, because the second overwrites the first with the same bytes.

## Python

The two deliveries.

```{.python .run}
writes = {}
def work(msg, crash):
    writes[msg] = writes.get(msg, 0) + 1   # the thumbnail is written
    return not crash                       # acknowledged only if no crash
queue = ["photo:7"]
acked = work(queue[0], crash=True)
if not acked: acked = work(queue[0], crash=False)
print("writes of photo:7:", writes["photo:7"], "| acknowledged:", acked)
```

```{.text .run-output}
writes of photo:7: 2 | acknowledged: True
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise orders work by priority instead of arrival. Liu describes an in-memory heap.

::: {#exr-wq-priority}
#### A priority queue

Liu's in-memory priority queue keeps "the event with the highest priority" at the root of a max heap [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Custom Queue"]. Thumbnails of paying users have priority $2$, others $1$. In what order are five messages processed, and what risk does a
steady stream of priority-$2$ messages create?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By priority, and by arrival within a priority. A steady stream of priority-$2$ messages starves priority $1$: Tan notes of RabbitMQ's
priority queues that there is "no concept of fairness or consideration of starvation" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 4.6.3, p. 97].

## Python

A heap keyed by minus the priority and the arrival number.

```{.python .run}
import heapq
arrivals = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 1), ("d", 2), ("e", 1)]
heap = []
for n, (msg, prio) in enumerate(arrivals):
    heapq.heappush(heap, (-prio, n, msg))
print([heapq.heappop(heap)[2] for _ in range(len(heap))])
```

```{.text .run-output}
['b', 'd', 'a', 'c', 'e']
```
::::
:::

::::

### How a backlog grows and drains

A queue absorbs a burst by growing. How fast it grows and how fast it drains are differences of rates, and @fig-bl-burst shows both.

![Backlog of a queue during and after a burst: the fluid model's line and one simulation with random arrivals and processing times. The backlog
grows at the excess of arrivals over capacity and drains at the spare capacity.](figures/backlog.svg){#fig-bl-burst width=80%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-backlog}
#### Backlog of a queue under a burst

Let messages arrive at an empty queue at rate $\lambda_1$ during $[0, \Delta]$ and at rate $\lambda_0$ afterwards, and let $c$ workers, each
completing $\mu$ messages per unit time while busy, process them in order of arrival. In the **fluid model** arrivals and departures are continuous:
the arrivals by time $t$ are $A(t) = \int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du$, the departures $D(t)$ have rate $c\mu$ while the backlog $B(t) = A(t) - D(t)$ is
positive and rate $\min(\lambda(t), c\mu)$ while it is zero.

(a) If $\lambda_1 \leq c\mu$ the backlog stays zero. If $\lambda_1 > c\mu$, then $B(t) = (\lambda_1 - c\mu)t$ for $0 \leq t \leq \Delta$, so
the backlog peaks at $(\lambda_1 - c\mu)\Delta$.

(b) After a burst with $\lambda_1 > c\mu$: if $\lambda_0 < c\mu$, the backlog falls at rate $c\mu - \lambda_0$ and is zero from time
$\Delta + (\lambda_1 - c\mu)\Delta/(c\mu - \lambda_0)$ on; if $\lambda_0 \geq c\mu$, it never falls, and if $\lambda_0 > c\mu$ then
$B(t)/t \to \lambda_0 - c\mu$.

(c) A message arriving at time $t$ waits $B(t)/(c\mu)$ before its processing begins.

(d) For random arrivals, recalled from chapter 3: if arrivals form a Poisson process of rate $\lambda < c\mu$ and processing times are independent
and $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$, the stationary mean backlog is $L = C(c, a)\rho/(1 - \rho) + a$ and the mean time in the system is
$W = C(c, a)/(c\mu - \lambda) + 1/\mu$, with $a = \lambda/\mu$ and $\rho = a/c$ (@thm-erlang-c); for $c = 1$ these are $L = \rho/(1 - \rho)$
and $W = 1/(\mu - \lambda)$ (@thm-mm1). Both grow without bound as $\rho \to 1$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) While $B = 0$ and $\lambda(t) \leq c\mu$, the departure rate is $\min(\lambda, c\mu) = \lambda$, equal to the arrival rate, so $B$
stays zero. If $\lambda_1 > c\mu$, the departure rate is $c\mu$ whether $B$ is zero or positive, so $B'(t) = \lambda_1 - c\mu > 0$ on
$[0, \Delta]$ and $B(t) = (\lambda_1 - c\mu)t$ from $B(0) = 0$.

(b) After $\Delta$, while $B > 0$, $B'(t) = \lambda_0 - c\mu$. If $\lambda_0 < c\mu$, $B$ falls linearly from $(\lambda_1 - c\mu)\Delta$ and
reaches zero after $(\lambda_1 - c\mu)\Delta/(c\mu - \lambda_0)$; from then on it stays zero by the argument of (a). If $\lambda_0 \geq c\mu$,
$B' = \lambda_0 - c\mu \geq 0$ while $B > 0$, so $B$ never falls and stays positive; then $B(t) = B(\Delta) + (\lambda_0 - c\mu)(t - \Delta)$ and
$B(t)/t \to \lambda_0 - c\mu$.

(c) In order of arrival, the message arriving at $t$ starts once the $B(t)$ messages ahead of it are done. Until then the backlog is positive, so
they are done at rate $c\mu$, in time $B(t)/(c\mu)$.

(d) These are parts (b) and (c) of @thm-erlang-c, with $L = L_q + a$ since the mean number in processing is $a$, and parts (b) and (c) of
@thm-mm1; they are proved there. $\square$

Parts (a) to (c) say that capacity between the mean and the peak rate is enough if the delay of (c) is acceptable; part (d) says that even below
capacity, random arrivals keep a backlog, which is why utilisation is kept well below one.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The thumbnail pool meets the busiest hour with less than peak capacity. Parts (a) and (b) give the cost.

::: {#exm-bl-peak-hour}
#### The busiest hour

With $c = 120$ workers of $\mu = 5$ per second, capacity is $600$ per second against $\lambda_1 = 694$ for $\Delta = 3600\,\mathrm{s}$. The
backlog peaks at $(694 - 600) \cdot 3600 = 3.4 \times 10^5$ messages, and after the hour, at the mean rate $\lambda_0 = 231$, it drains in
$3.4 \times 10^5/368.5 = 923\,\mathrm{s}$.

```{.python .run}
lam1, lam0, c, mu, Delta = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 2e7 / 86400, 120, 5, 3600
peak = (lam1 - c * mu) * Delta
print(f"peak backlog {peak:.3g}, drained {peak / (c * mu - lam0):.0f} s after the hour")
```

```{.text .run-output}
peak backlog 3.4e+05, drained 923 s after the hour
```
:::

Part (c) turns a backlog into a delay. The last upload of the hour waits longest.

::: {#exm-bl-wait}
#### How late the last thumbnail is

At the end of the hour of @exm-bl-peak-hour the backlog is $3.4 \times 10^5$, so an upload then waits $3.4 \times 10^5/600 = 567\,\mathrm{s}$,
nine and a half minutes, for its thumbnail.

```{.python .run}
B, cap = (3 * 2e7 / 86400 - 600) * 3600, 600
print(f"wait {B / cap:.0f} s = {B / cap / 60:.1f} min")
```

```{.text .run-output}
wait 567 s = 9.4 min
```
:::

With $150$ workers the fluid model sees no backlog at the peak. Part (d) sees one.

::: {#exm-bl-random}
#### A backlog below capacity

At $\lambda = 694$, $\mu = 5$ and $c = 150$, the fluid backlog is zero, but with Poisson arrivals and exponential times the utilisation is
$\rho = 0.926$ and @thm-erlang-c gives the mean backlog and time in the system computed below.

```{.python .run}
import math
def erlang_c(c, a):
    B = 1.0
    for k in range(1, c + 1): B = a * B / (k + a * B)   # Erlang B by recursion
    return c * B / (c - a * (1 - B))
lam, mu, c = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 5.0, 150
a = lam / mu; rho = a / c; C = erlang_c(c, a)
print(f"rho {rho:.3f}, P(wait) {C:.3f}, L {C * rho / (1 - rho) + a:.1f}, W {C / (c * mu - lam) + 1 / mu:.3f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
rho 0.926, P(wait) 0.259, L 142.1, W 0.205 s
```
:::

A simulation with random arrivals and times follows the fluid line. The run uses SimPy at a small scale.

::: {#exm-bl-simpy}
#### A simulated burst

Four workers of rate $1$ face $\lambda_1 = 6$ for $100$ time units, then $\lambda_0 = 2$. The fluid model predicts a peak of $200$ at $t = 100$
and an empty queue at $t = 200$; the seeded simulation is close.

```{.python .run}
import random, simpy
random.seed(4)
env = simpy.Environment()
pool = simpy.Resource(env, capacity=4)
state = {"B": 0, "trace": []}
def job(env):
    with pool.request() as req:
        yield req
        yield env.timeout(random.expovariate(1.0))
    state["B"] -= 1
def source(env):
    while True:
        rate = 6 if env.now < 100 else 2
        yield env.timeout(random.expovariate(rate))
        state["B"] += 1
        env.process(job(env))
def watch(env):
    while True:
        state["trace"].append((env.now, state["B"])); yield env.timeout(1)
env.process(source(env)); env.process(watch(env)); env.run(until=300)
B100 = dict(state["trace"])[100]
empty = next(t for t, b in state["trace"] if t > 100 and b <= 4)
print("backlog at t=100:", B100, "| first t>100 with at most 4 present:", empty)
```

```{.text .run-output}
backlog at t=100: 189 | first t>100 with at most 4 present: 194
```
:::

Xu adds workers when the queue grows. Part (b) says how much that shortens the drain.

::: {#exm-bl-xu-workers}
#### Adding workers

Doubling the pool of @exm-bl-peak-hour to $240$ workers at the end of the hour raises the spare capacity from $368.5$ to $968.5$ per second and cuts the
drain from $923$ to $351\,\mathrm{s}$; doubling it at the start of the hour avoids the backlog, since $1200 > 694$.

```{.python .run}
B, lam0 = (3 * 2e7 / 86400 - 600) * 3600, 2e7 / 86400
for c in (120, 240):
    print(c, "workers: drain", round(B / (5 * c - lam0)), "s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
120 workers: drain 923 s
240 workers: drain 351 s
```
:::

Tan names the benefit that parts (a) and (b) measure. The queue lets capacity sit below the peak.

::: {#exm-bl-tan-smooth}
#### Smoothing uneven traffic

Queues "can be used to smooth out uneven traffic, preventing our service from being overloaded by traffic spikes, and keeping our service
cost-efficient, because we do not need to provision a large number of hosts just to handle periods of high traffic" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024,
Sec. 4.6.3, p. 96]. The price is the delay of part (c), and the condition is part (b)'s $\lambda_0 < c\mu$: the traffic after the spike must leave
spare capacity.
:::

Liu warns about consumers that are too slow. It is the second case of part (b).

::: {#exm-bl-liu-backlog}
#### A backlog that never drains

"If the calculation is compute-intensive, it could cause the streaming to backlog the data since the consumption isn't fast enough for the data
production rate" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Batch vs Stream Processing"]. With $\lambda_0 > c\mu$ the backlog grows at
$\lambda_0 - c\mu$ for ever, whatever buffer holds it.
:::

Part (d) with one worker shows how fast waits grow. The mean time in the system is $1/(\mu - \lambda)$.

::: {#exm-bl-mm1-curve}
#### Waits near saturation

One worker of $\mu = 5$ per second gives the mean times below. Going from $\rho = 0.9$ to $0.99$ multiplies the mean time by ten.

```{.python .run}
mu = 5.0
for rho in (0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99):
    print(f"rho {rho}: L {rho / (1 - rho):6.1f}, W {1 / (mu - rho * mu):6.2f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
rho 0.5: L    1.0, W   0.40 s
rho 0.8: L    4.0, W   1.00 s
rho 0.9: L    9.0, W   2.00 s
rho 0.95: L   19.0, W   4.00 s
rho 0.99: L   99.0, W  20.00 s
```
:::

A queue can bound waits by dropping old messages. Reis describes the trade-off.

::: {#exm-bl-reis-ttl}
#### A backlog that expires

A message's time to live is "how long you want events to live before they are acknowledged and ingested"; "an extremely short TTL ... might cause
most messages to disappear before processing. A very long TTL (several weeks or months) will create a backlog of many unprocessed messages,
resulting in long wait times" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 7, p. 248]. By part (c), a TTL $\theta$ drops the messages that arrive when
$B(t) > c\mu\theta$.
:::

Little's law holds for any queue, random or not. The run checks it on a simulated pool.

::: {#exm-bl-little-check}
#### Little's law in the simulation

For the pool of @exm-bl-simpy at the constant rate $\lambda = 3$, the time-average backlog and $\lambda$ times the mean time in the system agree,
as @thm-littles-law says.

```{.python .run}
import random, simpy
random.seed(5)
env = simpy.Environment(); pool = simpy.Resource(env, capacity=4)
times, area = [], {"a": 0.0, "B": 0, "t": 0.0}
def tick(env):
    area["a"] += area["B"] * (env.now - area["t"]); area["t"] = env.now
def job(env):
    t0 = env.now
    with pool.request() as req:
        yield req; yield env.timeout(random.expovariate(1.0))
    tick(env); area["B"] -= 1; times.append(env.now - t0)
def source(env):
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(random.expovariate(3.0)); tick(env); area["B"] += 1; env.process(job(env))
env.process(source(env)); env.run(until=20000)
tick(env)
print(f"time-average backlog {area['a'] / env.now:.3f}, lambda x mean time {3.0 * sum(times) / len(times):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
time-average backlog 4.575, lambda x mean time 4.565
```
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise changes the pool in the middle of a burst. The proof of part (b) applies piece by piece.

::: {#exr-bl-more-workers}
#### Workers added during the burst

In @exm-bl-peak-hour, $60$ more workers join $30$ minutes into the hour. Find the peak backlog and when the queue is empty.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For $1800\,\mathrm{s}$ the backlog grows at $94$ per second, to $1.7 \times 10^5$. With $180$ workers capacity is $900 > 694$, so it falls at $205.6$
per second, and is empty after $1.7 \times 10^5/205.6 = 827\,\mathrm{s}$ more, at $2627\,\mathrm{s}$, before the hour ends; the peak is at $30$ minutes.

## Python

The pieces, and an Euler integration of the fluid model.

```{.python .run}
lam1 = 3 * 2e7 / 86400
B1 = (lam1 - 600) * 1800
print(f"peak {B1:.3g} at 1800 s, empty at {1800 + B1 / (900 - lam1):.0f} s")
B, t, dt = 0.0, 0.0, 0.1
while t < 3600:
    cap = 600 if t < 1800 else 900
    B = max(0.0, B + (lam1 - cap) * dt); t += dt
    if t > 1800 and B == 0: break
print(f"integration: empty at {t:.0f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
peak 1.7e+05 at 1800 s, empty at 2627 s
integration: empty at 2627 s
```
::::
:::

The second exercise inverts part (c). A wait bound sets the capacity.

::: {#exr-bl-capacity-for-wait}
#### Capacity for a bounded wait

Show that the wait of every message in the burst of part (a) is at most $w$ if and only if $c\mu \geq \lambda_1\Delta/(\Delta + w)$. How many
workers keep thumbnails at most a minute late in the busiest hour?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The longest wait is at $t = \Delta$, $(\lambda_1 - c\mu)\Delta/(c\mu)$ by (a) and (c) (or zero if $\lambda_1 \leq c\mu$). It is at most $w$ if and
only if $\lambda_1\Delta \leq c\mu(\Delta + w)$. With $\lambda_1 = 694$, $\Delta = 3600$ and $w = 60$, $c\mu \geq 683$: $137$ workers.

## Python

The bound and a check.

```{.python .run}
import math
lam1, Delta, w, mu = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 3600, 60, 5
cap = lam1 * Delta / (Delta + w); c = math.ceil(cap / mu)
print(f"capacity {cap:.1f}/s -> {c} workers; longest wait {(lam1 - c * mu) * Delta / (c * mu):.1f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
capacity 683.1/s -> 137 workers; longest wait 49.6 s
```
::::
:::

The third exercise asks for the first claim of part (a) for any arrival rate. The fluid model never builds a queue it can serve.

::: {#exr-bl-zero-proof}
#### No backlog below capacity

Prove that if $\lambda(t) \leq c\mu$ for all $t$, the fluid backlog stays zero, for any integrable arrival rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Suppose $B(t_1) > 0$ for some $t_1$, and let $t_0 = \sup\{t < t_1 : B(t) = 0\}$, so $B(t_0) = 0$ by continuity and $B > 0$ on $(t_0, t_1]$. On that
interval the departure rate is $c\mu$, so $B(t_1) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1}(\lambda(u) - c\mu)\,du \leq 0$, a contradiction.

## Python

An Euler integration with a rate that touches capacity.

```{.python .run}
import math
cmu, B, dt = 10.0, 0.0, 0.001
worst = 0.0
for k in range(100000):
    lam = cmu * (0.5 + 0.5 * math.sin(k * dt))     # between 0 and c mu
    B = max(0.0, B + (lam - cmu) * dt); worst = max(worst, B)
print("largest backlog:", worst)
```

```{.text .run-output}
largest backlog: 0.0
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise follows a whole day. Capacity below the peak but above the mean leaves a backlog only around the peak.

::: {#exr-bl-daily}
#### A day of uploads

Let uploads arrive at $\lambda(t) = 231\,(1 + 0.9\sin(2\pi t/86400))$ per second, and let the pool have capacity $300$. Integrate the fluid
model over two days and find the largest backlog and the longest wait.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The backlog grows while $\lambda(t) > 300$, a few hours around the peak, and drains afterwards; the run finds the peak backlog and, by part (c),
the longest wait. Over the second day the pattern repeats, since the queue empties each day.

## Python

Euler integration with a step of one second.

```{.python .run}
import math
cap, B, worst = 300.0, 0.0, 0.0
for t in range(2 * 86400):
    lam = 231 * (1 + 0.9 * math.sin(2 * math.pi * t / 86400))
    B = max(0.0, B + lam - cap); worst = max(worst, B)
print(f"peak backlog {worst:.3g}, longest wait {worst / cap / 60:.0f} min, backlog at the end {B:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
peak backlog 3.05e+06, longest wait 170 min, backlog at the end 0
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise uses the last case of part (b). A queue whose rate exceeds capacity fills any buffer.

::: {#exr-bl-unbounded}
#### When the memory runs out

After a deployment the thumbnail workers slow to $\mu = 2$ per second while uploads stay at $231$ per second and $c = 100$. A broker can hold
$10^6$ messages. When is it full, and what happens then?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Capacity is $200 < 231$, so the backlog grows at $31.5$ per second and reaches $10^6$ after $3.2 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{s}$, $8.8$ hours. Then the
broker must refuse or drop messages: the queue only delayed the failure.

## Python

The time to fill.

```{.python .run}
lam0, cap, limit = 2e7 / 86400, 100 * 2, 1e6
print(f"growth {lam0 - cap:.1f}/s, full after {limit / (lam0 - cap):.0f} s = {limit / (lam0 - cap) / 3600:.1f} h")
```

```{.text .run-output}
growth 31.5/s, full after 31765 s = 8.8 h
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks part (c) by simulation. The message arriving at the end of the burst should wait about $B/(c\mu)$.

::: {#exr-bl-simpy-wait}
#### The wait at the end of the burst

In the setting of @exm-bl-simpy, measure the wait of messages arriving just before $t = 100$ and compare with $B(100)/(c\mu) = 50$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The fluid model predicts $200/4 = 50$. The simulated waits of messages arriving in $[99, 100]$ are close to it; the difference is the randomness
that part (d) describes.

## Python

SimPy with waiting times recorded.

```{.python .run}
import random, simpy
random.seed(4)
env = simpy.Environment(); pool = simpy.Resource(env, capacity=4)
waits = []
def job(env):
    t0 = env.now
    with pool.request() as req:
        yield req
        if 99 <= t0 <= 100: waits.append(env.now - t0)
        yield env.timeout(random.expovariate(1.0))
def source(env):
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(random.expovariate(6 if env.now < 100 else 2)); env.process(job(env))
env.process(source(env)); env.run(until=400)
print(f"{len(waits)} messages, mean wait {sum(waits) / len(waits):.1f} (fluid model 50)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
7 messages, mean wait 43.5 (fluid model 50)
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise sizes the pool by part (d). The mean wait must be under a second.

::: {#exr-bl-erlang-pool}
#### Workers for a one-second wait

With Poisson uploads at $694$ per second and exponential thumbnail times of mean $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$, find the smallest pool with a mean wait
$W_q \leq 1\,\mathrm{s}$, and with $W_q \leq 0.01\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$W_q = C(c, a)/(c\mu - \lambda)$ (@thm-erlang-c) falls quickly once $c$ passes $a = 138.8$; the search below finds the two pools. The second needs
only a few more workers than the first: large pools are efficient.

## Python

A search over $c$.

```{.python .run}
import math
def erlang_c(c, a):
    B = 1.0
    for k in range(1, c + 1): B = a * B / (k + a * B)   # Erlang B by recursion
    return c * B / (c - a * (1 - B))
lam, mu = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 5.0
a = lam / mu
for target in (1.0, 0.01):
    c = math.floor(a) + 1
    while erlang_c(c, a) / (c * mu - lam) > target: c += 1
    print(f"W_q <= {target}: c = {c}, rho = {a / c:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
W_q <= 1.0: c = 140, rho = 0.992
W_q <= 0.01: c = 147, rho = 0.945
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise looks at $\lambda = c\mu$. The fluid model sees no backlog; randomness makes one that grows like a square root.

::: {#exr-bl-critical}
#### Exactly at capacity

Simulate a single queue with arrivals and service both Bernoulli with probability $1/2$ per step, for $T$ steps. How does the mean backlog at
time $T$ grow with $T$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The backlog is a random walk with zero drift, held at zero from below. The run shows its mean growing in proportion to $\sqrt T$, about
$0.54\sqrt T$, far from the fluid model's zero: at capacity the fluid model is wrong by an amount that grows without bound.

## Python

Many walks with NumPy.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
for T in (100, 400, 1600):
    B = np.zeros(2000)
    for _ in range(T):
        B = np.maximum(0, B + rng.integers(0, 2, 2000) - rng.integers(0, 2, 2000))
    print(f"T {T}: mean backlog {B.mean():.1f}, divided by sqrt(T) {B.mean() / np.sqrt(T):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
T 100: mean backlog 5.2, divided by sqrt(T) 0.52
T 400: mean backlog 10.9, divided by sqrt(T) 0.54
T 1600: mean backlog 21.5, divided by sqrt(T) 0.54
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise prices Liu's buffering. A per-request overhead is shared by a batch.

::: {#exr-bl-batching}
#### Batching raises capacity

Each request to the broker costs $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ plus $0.1\,\mathrm{ms}$ per message. Find a producer's capacity with batches of $1$ and of $50$,
and the extra delay of waiting to fill a batch of $50$ at $694$ messages per second. Kafka reports that "a batch size of 50 messages improved the
throughput by almost an order of magnitude" [@kreps2011kafka, Sec. 5].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A batch of $b$ takes $5 + 0.1b\,\mathrm{ms}$, so capacity is $b/(5 + 0.1b)$ per ms: $196$ per second for $b = 1$ and $5000$ for $b = 50$, a factor of
$25$ in this model. Filling a batch of $50$ takes $50/694 = 72\,\mathrm{ms}$: Liu's trade-off, "the longer you wait, the less overhead you incur per
request", against freshness [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Buffering"].

## Python

The two capacities and the fill time.

```{.python .run}
for b in (1, 50):
    print(f"batch {b}: {1000 * b / (5 + 0.1 * b):.0f} messages/s")
print(f"fill time for 50 at 694/s: {1000 * 50 / 694:.0f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
batch 1: 196 messages/s
batch 50: 5000 messages/s
fill time for 50 at 694/s: 72 ms
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise puts two bursts close together. The second starts on top of what the first left.

::: {#exr-bl-two-bursts}
#### Two bursts

Two bursts of $\lambda_1 = 694$ for $1800\,\mathrm{s}$ are separated by $600\,\mathrm{s}$ at $\lambda_0 = 231$, with capacity $600$. Find the
backlog at the end of the second burst and compare with one burst of $3600\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The first burst leaves $94.4 \times 1800 = 1.70 \times 10^5$; the gap removes $368.5 \times 600 = 2.2 \times 10^5$, more than that, so the queue is empty
when the second burst starts and ends it at $1.70 \times 10^5$ again: half the single burst's $3.4 \times 10^5$. Had the gap been shorter than
$1.70 \times 10^5/368.5 = 461\,\mathrm{s}$, the bursts would have added.

## Python

The three phases.

```{.python .run}
lam1, lam0, cap = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 2e7 / 86400, 600
B = (lam1 - cap) * 1800
B = max(0.0, B - (cap - lam0) * 600)
B += (lam1 - cap) * 1800
print(f"two bursts: {B:.3g}; one burst: {(lam1 - cap) * 3600:.3g}; shortest gap that empties: {(lam1 - cap) * 1800 / (cap - lam0):.0f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
two bursts: 1.7e+05; one burst: 3.4e+05; shortest gap that empties: 461 s
```
::::
:::

::::

## Publish-subscribe and topics {#sec-pubsub}

A queue gives each message to one consumer; many messages are of interest to several. Sinha describes the other pattern: "messages are published by
producers (publishers) on a specific topic and consumers (subscribers) receive messages based on their subscription to those topics. This model
is highly effective for broadcasting information to multiple consumers" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 7, "Designing a pub/sub system"]. This
section defines topics, subscriptions, push and pull, and retention, and compares queues with topics.

For more on this topic, see @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 7, "Designing a pub/sub system"], @gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024 [Ch. 3,
pp. 86-89], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 4.6.2-4.6.3, pp. 95-97], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Publisher Subscriber"] and
@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Ch. 5, pp. 179-180].

### Topics, subscriptions, push and pull

A topic copies each message to every subscription, and each subscription is drained like a queue. @fig-ps-topologies draws the two arrangements.

![A queue shared by a pool of workers, and a topic whose messages are copied to every subscription. Each subscription has its own consumers and its
own backlog.](figures/topologies.svg){#fig-ps-topologies width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-pubsub}
#### Topics and publish-subscribe

1. A **topic** is a named channel to which **publishers** send messages. A **subscriber** registers a **subscription** to a topic and receives
   every message published to it from then on. **Publish-subscribe** delivers each message to every subscription; a **point-to-point** queue
   delivers it to one consumer.
2. Each subscription keeps its own backlog and acknowledgements, so a topic with $S$ subscriptions delivers each message $S$ times, and
   subscriptions progress independently.
3. In **push** delivery the broker sends messages to the consumer; in **pull** delivery the consumer asks the broker for messages when it is ready.
4. A broker either removes a message once every subscription has acknowledged it, or **retains** it for a fixed **retention period** whatever has
   been consumed.
:::

::::

Kafka offers both delivery models of item 1: "the point-to-point delivery model in which multiple consumers jointly consume a single copy of all
messages in a topic, as well as the publish/subscribe model in which multiple consumers each retrieve its own copy of a topic" [@kreps2011kafka,
Sec. 3]. Item 2's independence is Liu's: "each subscriber can behave independently from other subscribers" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Publisher Subscriber"].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Gandhi presents the choice with a trading service and two consumers. A queue is point-to-point, a topic a broadcast.

::: {#exm-ps-gandhi-models}
#### Queues and topics in Gandhi

With a queue, "the publisher knows who is receiving the message. To reach multiple consumers, the publisher needs to send a message to one
queue for each consumer"; with a topic, "the publisher simply produces and sends a message ... The publisher doesn't know (or care) how many
services are listening" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3, p. 86]. A topic with one subscription per consumer delivers the same messages as
one queue per consumer; what differs is who knows the list of consumers.
:::

Gandhi lists what queues give. Each item follows from the publisher knowing its consumers.

::: {#exm-ps-gandhi-queues}
#### The case for queues

Queues support "heterogeneous messages for different consumers", allow "independent monitoring and scaling", and are "more secure"; against
that they have a "higher degree of coupling (hurts extensibility)", the trading service "must connect to multiple queues", and they need
"additional infrastructure" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3, p. 88].
:::

Topics trade the other way. Low coupling comes with one message for all.

::: {#exm-ps-gandhi-topics}
#### The case for topics

Topics have "low coupling (helps extensibility)" and one place to publish, but a "homogeneous message for all services", one thing to monitor and
scale, and are "less secure", since "anyone can subscribe to the topic without the trading service knowing" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3,
p. 89]. Gandhi's conclusion is the first law of software architecture, "it depends!": the sneaker company needs extensibility, so it picks topics
[@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3, p. 90].
:::

An upload interests several services. A topic serves them all without the upload handler knowing them.

::: {#exm-ps-photo-topic}
#### The photo service's upload topic

The upload handler publishes "photo $x$ uploaded by user $u$" to a topic with four subscriptions: thumbnails, feed, search and notifications. At
the peak the topic delivers $4 \times 694 = 2778$ messages per second, $2.8\,\mathrm{MB/s}$ of $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ messages, and a fifth service
can subscribe without a change to the handler.

```{.python .run}
lam, size = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 1e3
subs = ["thumbnails", "feed", "search", "notifications"]
print(f"{len(subs) * lam:.0f} deliveries/s, {len(subs) * lam * size / 1e6:.1f} MB/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
2778 deliveries/s, 2.8 MB/s
```
:::

Item 2 is easy to model. Each subscription is its own queue.

::: {#exm-ps-code}
#### A topic in code

Publishing appends to every subscription's queue; consuming one subscription does not touch the others.

```{.python .run}
from collections import deque
subs = {"feed": deque(), "search": deque()}
def publish(msg):
    for q in subs.values(): q.append(msg)
for i in range(3): publish(f"upload:{i}")
subs["feed"].popleft(); subs["feed"].popleft()       # the feed consumer is fast
print({name: list(q) for name, q in subs.items()})
```

```{.text .run-output}
{'feed': ['upload:2'], 'search': ['upload:0', 'upload:1', 'upload:2']}
```
:::

Liu's pub/sub broker deletes a message once it is processed. It is the first case of item 4.

::: {#exm-ps-liu-ack}
#### Remove after acknowledgement

"Once the consumer successfully processes the event, the consumer will send an acknowledgment to the queue, and the queue will remove the event
... Unlike a message queue like Kafka, there's no retention period for the message"; this fits a ride request, since "10 minutes later, that request
is no longer relevant" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Publisher Subscriber"].
:::

Tan prefers pull in general. The consumer sets its own pace.

::: {#exm-ps-tan-pull}
#### Pull protects the consumer

"In pull, the consumer controls the rate of message consumption and will not be overloaded"; push is better where many data sources would need
crawlers, and in "lossy applications like audio and video live-streaming" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 4.6.2, p. 96].
:::

Kafka chose pull for the same reason. It adds a second one.

::: {#exm-ps-kafka-pull}
#### Why Kafka pulls

Kafka finds pull "more suitable for our applications since each consumer can retrieve the messages at the maximum rate it can sustain and avoid
being flooded by messages pushed faster than it can handle. The pull model also makes it easy to rewind a consumer" [@kreps2011kafka, Sec. 2].
:::

A topic can feed operational and analytical consumers at once. Reis's example is web orders.

::: {#exm-ps-reis-orders}
#### One topic, two kinds of consumer

A web orders topic is sent "to a couple of consumers, such as fulfillment and marketing ... The fulfillment subscriber will use events to trigger
a fulfillment process, while marketing runs real-time analytics"; "a topic can have zero, one, or multiple producers and customers"
[@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 5, p. 180].
:::

Tan compares two brokers along item 4. The difference decides whether a consumer can read a message again.

::: {#exm-ps-tan-table}
#### Delete on dequeue or retain

In Kafka "events on the queue are not removed after consumption, so the same event can be consumed repeatedly", with a retention period "seven
days by default"; in RabbitMQ "messages on the queue are removed upon dequeuing, as per the definition of 'queue'" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024,
Sec. 4.6.3, Table 4.1, p. 97].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise follows item 1's \"from then on\". A subscription made after a message misses it.

::: {#exr-ps-late}
#### A late subscriber

A search service subscribes to the upload topic after three uploads have been published. Which uploads does it receive, with a broker that removes
acknowledged messages and with one that retains them for a week?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A subscription receives messages published from then on, so it misses the three in both cases. A retaining broker still holds them, so the
search service can read them separately; a deleting broker has removed them once the existing subscriptions acknowledged them.

## Python

Two brokers.

```{.python .run}
log, subs = [], {"feed": []}
def publish(m):
    log.append(m)
    for q in subs.values(): q.append(m)
for i in range(3): publish(f"u{i}")
subs["search"] = []
publish("u3")
print("search receives:", subs["search"], "| retained, readable again:", log)
```

```{.text .run-output}
search receives: ['u3'] | retained, readable again: ['u0', 'u1', 'u2', 'u3']
```
::::
:::

The second exercise counts the bytes a topic sends. Each subscription multiplies them.

::: {#exr-ps-egress}
#### Egress grows with subscriptions

Find the broker's outgoing bandwidth for the upload topic at the peak with $S = 1, 4, 16$ subscriptions and $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ messages, and with
$2\,\mathrm{MB}$ messages if the photo itself were published.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Item 2 gives $S\lambda s$: with $1\,\mathrm{kB}$, $0.7$, $2.8$ and $11\,\mathrm{MB/s}$; with $2\,\mathrm{MB}$, $1.4$, $5.6$ and $22\,\mathrm{GB/s}$. Large payloads
belong in object storage, with only their identifier in the message, as Pacheco advises: "Kafka is not a file server"
[@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024, Ch. 8, "Apache Kafka"].

## Python

The products.

```{.python .run}
lam = 3 * 2e7 / 86400
for s, unit, div in ((1e3, "MB/s", 1e6), (2e6, "GB/s", 1e9)):
    print([f"S={S}: {S * lam * s / div:.1f} {unit}" for S in (1, 4, 16)])
```

```{.text .run-output}
['S=1: 0.7 MB/s', 'S=4: 2.8 MB/s', 'S=16: 11.1 MB/s']
['S=1: 1.4 GB/s', 'S=4: 5.6 GB/s', 'S=16: 22.2 GB/s']
```
::::
:::

The third exercise applies Gandhi's trade-off tables. Each requirement favours one side.

::: {#exr-ps-requirements}
#### Queues or topics

Gandhi asks which option fits each requirement: "Security is important to us", "Different downstream services need different kinds of
information", "We'll be adding other downstream services in the future" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3, p. 89]. Answer from the tables of
@exm-ps-gandhi-queues and @exm-ps-gandhi-topics.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Security: queues, which are "more secure". Different information: queues, which support "heterogeneous messages". More services later: topics,
which have "low coupling". The answers come from the two tables; a design with all three requirements must rank them.

## Python

The tables as data.

```{.python .run}
pros = {"queues": {"security", "heterogeneous messages", "independent scaling"},
        "topics": {"extensibility", "one place to publish"}}
needs = {"security": "security", "different information": "heterogeneous messages", "more services later": "extensibility"}
for req, prop in needs.items():
    print(req, "->", [k for k, v in pros.items() if prop in v][0])
```

```{.text .run-output}
security -> queues
different information -> queues
more services later -> topics
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise checks item 2's independence. One subscription can fall behind alone.

::: {#exr-ps-slow}
#### A slow subscriber

The feed subscription processes $1000$ messages per second and the search subscription $500$, while the topic receives $694$. Find each backlog
after an hour.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each subscription is its own queue (item 2), so @prp-backlog applies to each: the feed's backlog stays zero, the search backlog grows at $194$ per
second to $7.0 \times 10^5$. The feed is unaffected.

## Python

The two backlogs.

```{.python .run}
lam = 3 * 2e7 / 86400
for name, cap in (("feed", 1000), ("search", 500)):
    print(name, f"{max(0, lam - cap) * 3600:.3g}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
feed 0
search 7e+05
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise compares push and pull with a consumer that is too slow. Push fills the consumer's buffer.

::: {#exr-ps-push-overflow}
#### Push into a slow consumer

A broker pushes $694$ messages per second to a consumer that processes $500$ and buffers $10^4$. When does the buffer overflow? What changes with
pull?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The buffer fills at $194$ per second, in $51\,\mathrm{s}$, after which messages are dropped or the consumer fails. With pull the consumer asks only
for what it can process, and the excess waits at the broker, as Kafka says (@exm-ps-kafka-pull); the backlog is the same, but it is held where
it is meant to be.

## Python

The fill time.

```{.python .run}
lam, cap, buf = 3 * 2e7 / 86400, 500, 1e4
print(f"overflow after {buf / (lam - cap):.0f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
overflow after 51 s
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise compares Gandhi's two set-ups when a consumer is added. The deliveries are the same; the change is elsewhere.

::: {#exr-ps-queue-per-consumer}
#### One queue per consumer

Model the trading service publishing to one queue per consumer and to a topic with one subscription per consumer. Add a compliance consumer and
count the changes to the trading service in each model.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Both deliver every trade to every consumer. With queues the trading service holds the list of queues and must add one; with a topic the compliance
service subscribes and the trading service is unchanged: "no need to make any changes to the trading service" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024,
Ch. 3, p. 89].

## Python

Both models.

```{.python .run}
queues = {"notification": [], "analytics": []}           # known to the publisher
topic_subs = {"notification": [], "analytics": []}       # known to the broker
publisher_config = list(queues)
queues["compliance"] = []; publisher_config.append("compliance")   # publisher changed
topic_subs["compliance"] = []                                      # publisher untouched
for q in publisher_config: queues[q].append("trade 1")
for q in topic_subs.values(): q.append("trade 1")
print("queues:", {k: len(v) for k, v in queues.items()}, "| topic:", {k: len(v) for k, v in topic_subs.items()})
print("publisher changes: queues 1, topic 0")
```

```{.text .run-output}
queues: {'notification': 1, 'analytics': 1, 'compliance': 1} | topic: {'notification': 1, 'analytics': 1, 'compliance': 1}
publisher changes: queues 1, topic 0
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise answers Gandhi's security objection. The broker can check subscriptions.

::: {#exr-ps-acl}
#### Who may subscribe

Gandhi counts against topics that "anyone can subscribe to the topic without the trading service knowing". What does an access list on
subscriptions change, and what does it not?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With an access list the broker refuses unknown subscribers, so the objection becomes a configuration of the broker instead of a property of
topics. The publisher still does not know who is subscribed; the list is managed by whoever runs the broker.

## Python

A broker with an access list.

```{.python .run}
allowed = {"notification", "analytics"}
subs = {}
def subscribe(name):
    if name not in allowed: return f"{name}: refused"
    subs[name] = []; return f"{name}: subscribed"
print([subscribe(n) for n in ("analytics", "rogue")])
```

```{.text .run-output}
['analytics: subscribed', 'rogue: refused']
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise sizes item 4's retention. Storage is rate times size times period.

::: {#exr-ps-retention-size}
#### What retention costs

Find the storage needed to retain a week of upload messages of $1\,\mathrm{kB}$, at $2 \times 10^7$ a day, with three replicas.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$2 \times 10^7 \times 10^3 \times 7 = 1.4 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{B}$, $140\,\mathrm{GB}$, and $420\,\mathrm{GB}$ with three replicas: small. Retention is
cheap for metadata messages; for photos it would be $2000$ times more.

## Python

The product.

```{.python .run}
per_day, size, days, N = 2e7, 1e3, 7, 3
print(f"{per_day * size * days / 1e9:.0f} GB, with replicas {N * per_day * size * days / 1e9:.0f} GB")
```

```{.text .run-output}
140 GB, with replicas 420 GB
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise checks a claim against the source's own table. A superset must have every feature.

::: {#exr-ps-tan-superset}
#### Is one broker a superset of the other?

Tan writes that Kafka "provides a superset of capabilities over RabbitMQ. In other words, Kafka can always be used in place of RabbitMQ but not
vice versa" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 4.6.3, p. 96]. Does Table 4.1 of the same section support this?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

No. The table lists for RabbitMQ "AMQP standard per-message queue priority", and for Kafka "No concept of priority" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024,
Sec. 4.6.3, Table 4.1, p. 97]. A design that needs priorities, such as @exr-wq-priority, cannot use Kafka in place of RabbitMQ without building
them itself, for example with one topic per priority.

## Python

The two feature sets from the table.

```{.python .run}
kafka = {"replication", "retention", "replay", "partitions"}
rabbit = {"per-message priority", "delete on dequeue", "replay"}
print("in RabbitMQ, not in Kafka:", sorted(rabbit - kafka))
```

```{.text .run-output}
in RabbitMQ, not in Kafka: ['delete on dequeue', 'per-message priority']
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise separates two terms that Tan joins. They deliver different numbers of copies.

::: {#exr-ps-tan-terms}
#### Producer/consumer or publish/subscribe

Tan writes "Producer/consumer aka publisher/subscriber or pub/sub, is an asynchronous messaging system that decouples services that produce
events from services that process events" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 4.6.2, p. 95]. Count the deliveries of one message to three consumers
in item 1's two models.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A point-to-point queue shared by three consumers delivers it once, to one of them; a topic with three subscriptions delivers it three times. Both
decouple producers from consumers, which is Tan's point, but they are different models; Tan's own definition of a message queue, processed "only
once by a single consumer", is the first.

## Python

Both models.

```{.python .run}
consumers = ["a", "b", "c"]
queue_deliveries = 1                     # one consumer takes it
topic_deliveries = len(consumers)        # every subscription gets a copy
print("queue:", queue_deliveries, "| topic:", topic_deliveries)
```

```{.text .run-output}
queue: 1 | topic: 3
```
::::
:::

::::

## Delivery semantics and idempotence {#sec-delivery}

A message can be lost, and it can be delivered twice; which of the two a system allows is a design decision. Liu's example is a queue of payments:
"Delivering more than once will cause an over-charge, and failing to deliver will result in undercharging" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Delivery Semantics and Guarantees"]. This section defines the three delivery semantics, idempotence and the end-to-end argument, and proves
when duplicate deliveries leave the same state as single ones.

For more on this topic, see @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Delivery Semantics and Guarantees" and "Idempotency"],
@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Ch. 4, "Order tolerance and idempotence", and Ch. 5, "Implementing idempotence and order
tolerance"], @saltzer1984end, @kreps2011kafka [Sec. 3.3] and @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Ch. 5, p. 179].

### At most once, at least once, effectively once

Delivery semantics count how often a message's effect happens. Idempotence makes the count harmless.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-delivery-semantics}
#### Delivery semantics, idempotence and the end-to-end argument

1. A messaging path gives **at-most-once** processing if the effect of each message occurs at most once and possibly never, **at-least-once**
   processing if it occurs at least once and possibly more often, and **exactly-once** processing if it occurs exactly once.
2. An operation $f$ on states is **idempotent** if applying it twice has the same result as applying it once: $f(f(s)) = f(s)$ for every state
   $s$.
3. An **idempotency key** is an identifier that a message carries, the same in every copy and every retry of it. A **deduplicating** consumer
   records the keys of the messages it has processed and skips any message whose key it has recorded. **Effectively-once** processing is
   at-least-once delivery to a deduplicating consumer, or to one whose effects are idempotent, so that each effect occurs once.
4. The **end-to-end argument** [@saltzer1984end, Introduction]: "The function in question can completely and correctly be implemented only with
   the knowledge and help of the application standing at the end points of the communication system. Therefore, providing that questioned
   function as a feature of the communication system itself is not possible. (Sometimes an incomplete version of the function provided by the
   communication system may be useful as a performance enhancement.)"
:::

::::

Item 1 is Liu's list [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Delivery Semantics and Guarantees"], and item 2 Reis's: "the outcome of processing
a message once is identical to the outcome of processing it multiple times" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 5, p. 179]. Item 3's
name "effectively once" is this chapter's; Liu describes the thing itself: "you can use at-least-once delivery and handle the idempotency on the
application level by having your data store for duplicate events" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Delivery Semantics and Guarantees"]. Items 2
and 3 carry the idempotent operations and idempotency keys of web interfaces (@def-web-api) over to messages.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Liu pairs each semantics with a use. The cost of a lost or a repeated effect decides.

::: {#exm-dl-liu-uses}
#### Which semantics for what

At most once suits "metrics collection like server health status" and a driver's location, since "you will get another update in 5-10 seconds";
at least once suits a job that "parses a file and saves it to the database", since writing "is idempotent based on file_id"; exactly once suits a
payment request to "a third party that does not handle idempotency" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Delivery Semantics and
Guarantees"].
:::

At most once is what happens when nobody retries. Liu describes both ends.

::: {#exm-dl-liu-at-most}
#### How at most once arises

The producer achieves it "by firing and forgetting", and on the consumer side "the consumer can poll the event and remove the message from the
queue. In the event of consumer failure, the system loses the message forever" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Delivery Semantics and
Guarantees"].
:::

At least once is what happens when everybody retries. A missing acknowledgement causes a duplicate.

::: {#exm-dl-liu-at-least}
#### How at least once arises

"When the consumer polls from the queue and commits the change but fails to acknowledge the queue, the event will be processed again when the
consumer retries"; on the producer side, a producer that resends after a lost acknowledgement "could duplicate data in the queue"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Delivery Semantics and Guarantees"].
:::

Liu's order quantity shows item 2 in an interface. Setting is idempotent, decrementing is not.

::: {#exm-dl-liu-quantity}
#### An idempotent and a non-idempotent call

`decrease_quantity(order, 1)` "isn't idempotent because if you call it multiple times, the quantity will keep decreasing", while
`update_quantity(order, 2)` "is idempotent because no matter how many times you call it, the quantity will still be 2"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Idempotency"].

```{.python .run}
decrease = lambda q: q - 1
update = lambda q: 2
q0 = 3
print("decrease once/twice:", decrease(q0), decrease(decrease(q0)), "| update once/twice:", update(q0), update(update(q0)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
decrease once/twice: 2 1 | update once/twice: 2 2
```
:::

The Kafka paper states its guarantee plainly. Duplicates are left to the application.

::: {#exm-dl-kafka}
#### Kafka promises at least once

"In general, Kafka only guarantees at-least-once delivery ... Most of the time, a message is delivered exactly once to each consumer group.
However, in the case when a consumer process crashes without a clean shutdown", its successor "may get some duplicate messages"; "If an application
cares about duplicates, it must add its own deduplication logic" [@kreps2011kafka, Sec. 3.3]. That is item 3.
:::

Even a broker that delivers once cannot see the consumer's effect. Reis gives the failure.

::: {#exm-dl-reis-ack}
#### Exactly-once delivery is not enough

"Even if our system can guarantee exactly-once delivery, a consumer might fully process a message but fail right before acknowledging
processing. The message will effectively be processed twice, but an idempotent system handles this scenario gracefully"
[@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 5, p. 179].
:::

Saltzer, Reed and Clark's first example is copying a file between hosts. Only an end-to-end check covers every threat.

::: {#exm-dl-careful-transfer}
#### Careful file transfer

The threats include disk faults, software mistakes in buffering, transient hardware errors, the network dropping or duplicating packets, and a
crash part way through. The cure is "end-to-end check and retry": the receiving host reads the copy back, "recalculates the checksum, and sends this
value back to host A ... Only if the two checksums agree does the file transfer application declare the transaction committed" [@saltzer1984end,
"End-to-end caretaking"]. A reliable network removes only one threat of five.
:::

A network's acknowledgement says a message arrived. The application wants to know it was acted on.

::: {#exm-dl-saltzer-ack}
#### What an acknowledgement means

"Knowing for sure that the message was delivered to the target host is not very important. What the application wants to know is whether or not the
target host acted on the message ... The acknowledgement that is really desired is an end-to-end one, which can be originated only by the target
application – 'I did it', or 'I didn't'" [@saltzer1984end, "Delivery guarantees"]. A broker's acknowledgement to a producer is of the first kind.
:::

Saltzer, Reed and Clark apply the argument to duplicates. The application makes some of them itself.

::: {#exm-dl-saltzer-dupes}
#### Duplicates the network cannot see

"Even if the network suppresses duplicates, the application itself may accidentally originate duplicate requests, in its own failure/retry
procedures. These application level duplications look like different messages to the communication system, so it cannot suppress them"
[@saltzer1984end, "Duplicate message suppression"]. A phone that retries an upload after a timeout sends a second request that the broker sees as
new; only a key chosen by the phone catches it.
:::

Gilbert makes the same point for identifiers. A server-generated identifier is not an idempotency key.

::: {#exm-dl-gilbert-ids}
#### Keys chosen by the client

With an auto-incrementing identifier, "if a client submits an HTTP POST request multiple times for the same logically unique domain entity payload,
then the service will create duplicate records ... The solution to this problem is to have the client generate the identifier and submit an HTTP PUT
request instead"; a random UUID "falls apart if the client forgets the UUID that it just generated" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 5,
"Deterministic identifiers"].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise chooses item 1's semantics for four messages. The cost of loss and of repetition decides each.

::: {#exr-dl-choose}
#### Semantics for the photo service

Choose a semantics for: a view-counter increment, a thumbnail job, a charge for a premium subscription, and a push notification of a new
follower.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

View counts: at most once, since a lost increment hardly matters and a cheap path is enough. Thumbnails: at least once, since rewriting a thumbnail
is idempotent. The charge: effectively once, with an idempotency key the payment provider accepts. Notifications: at least once, accepting a rare
duplicate, which Liu allows for notifications: "it may be ok to have the occasional minor end-user annoyance" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020,
Ch. 5, "Delivery Semantics and Guarantees"].

## Python

The choices as a table.

```{.python .run}
choice = {"view count": ("at most once", "loss is cheap"),
          "thumbnail": ("at least once", "rewriting is idempotent"),
          "premium charge": ("effectively once", "idempotency key at the provider"),
          "follower notification": ("at least once", "a rare duplicate is tolerable")}
for k, (sem, why) in choice.items(): print(f"{k:22s} {sem:17s} {why}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
view count             at most once      loss is cheap
thumbnail              at least once     rewriting is idempotent
premium charge         effectively once  idempotency key at the provider
follower notification  at least once     a rare duplicate is tolerable
```
::::
:::

The second exercise tests item 2 on six operations. Two checks on sample states settle each.

::: {#exr-dl-which-idempotent}
#### Which operations are idempotent

Which of these are idempotent: set $x = 5$; add $1$ to $x$; add an element to a set; append an element to a list; delete a key; set $x$ to
$\max(x, 7)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Setting, adding to a set, deleting and taking a maximum are idempotent: a second application finds the result already there. Adding $1$ and
appending are not: each application changes the state again.

## Python

The test $f(f(s)) = f(s)$ on a few states.

```{.python .run}
ops = {"set x=5": lambda s: {**s, "x": 5}, "x+=1": lambda s: {**s, "x": s["x"] + 1},
       "set add": lambda s: {**s, "S": s["S"] | {3}}, "list append": lambda s: {**s, "L": s["L"] + [3]},
       "delete k": lambda s: {k: v for k, v in s.items() if k != "k"}, "x=max(x,7)": lambda s: {**s, "x": max(s["x"], 7)}}
states = [{"x": x, "S": {1}, "L": [1], "k": 0} for x in (0, 9)]
for name, f in ops.items():
    print(f"{name:12s}", all(f(f(s)) == f(s) for s in states))
```

```{.text .run-output}
set x=5      True
x+=1         False
set add      True
list append  False
delete k     True
x=max(x,7)   True
```
::::
:::

The third exercise tests three candidate keys against a client retry. Only one is the same in every copy.

::: {#exr-dl-key-choice}
#### Which identifier is a key

A phone uploads a photo, times out and retries. Which of these catches the duplicate: the broker's message identifier, an identifier the phone
generated once and stored before the first attempt, a hash of the photo's bytes?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution
